summary:
Huánuco has no separate legal regime on gender identity; the department stands under Peru's national framework, and no source in the inventory records a Huánuco-specific provision, directive or enforcement action. The national position is therefore what a trans visitor to Huánuco will encounter.

Peru does not criminalise trans identity. What the national Congress has legislated is access to public facilities. In February 2025 the Comision de Mujer y Familia of the Congress approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante of Honor y Democracia, prohibiting entry into public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to a person's birth sex, with narrow exceptions for custody and for cases where required, such as accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities, and obliging venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs. The text still required plenary backing at that point, and the reported trigger was a July 2023 complaint about gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport.

The plenary approved the wider package on 2 April 2025 and waived a second vote: the Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents, whose Article 5.1 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary facility designated for a sex other than their birth sex. Inclusive signage, including wording such as 'women in their diversity', is banned by the same package. The restriction binds trans people and trans youth out of facilities matching their gender identity, and it reaches private venues as well as state premises.

Enforcement would rest on door and security staff. Activist and journalist Gianna Camacho, a trans human-rights defender, has argued that a guard checking a DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender is how the rule operates in practice. A consumer-protection body, INDECOPI, has already shown where such complaints land: SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against the gym chain SmartFit, which had assigned bathrooms on the basis of the sex recorded in the DNI. On television, Willax TV presenter Ana María Salcedo publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

The IDEHPUCP human-rights institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, analysing the provision on 15 April 2025 with Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte, reads Article 5 as a direct breach of Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

Hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip those provisions from the new code, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. Peru is one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Recorded violence against trans women is rising and under-counted. The annual report of the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia recorded 54 killings of LGBTI people and 170 rights-violation cases between 2020 and 2023: the homicide victims were 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian, with 19 killings in 2023 alone, 12 of them trans women. Killers were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides, and in 13 of the 19 killings in 2023. Among the cases is the February 2023 murder of trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano, 31, kidnapped from central Lima by the 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots; Priscila Aguado Huatuco, 30, was shot days earlier, and two killers were arrested in March 2023. The state does not incorporate sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an Article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.
tangentialFactors:
Gianna Camacho, co-author of the 2024 hate-crime reporting, has stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry, so the numbers above understate killings and rights violations of trans people across Peru.

Peru's position on LGBT coverage in hate-crime law is a regional outlier: only Paraguay and Guyana share the absence of such coverage in South America.

The Rojas Marín judgment is a comparative first for the Inter-American system, being the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, and it took close to two decades and litigation through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights to reach.

The bathroom restriction is a legislative development rather than settled practice, with the February 2025 dictamen still awaiting plenary approval before the April 2025 law carried the substance; the trigger cited for the bills was a July 2023 complaint over restroom labelling at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport, not an incident in Huánuco.

Compulsory transit screening has no reported basis in the sources: no source describes airport or roadblock screening of travellers by gender presentation in Huánuco, and the only identity-document check described in the inventory is venue-level, on a DNI at restroom doors.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition in Peru remains a long, costly and invasive process, according to the IDEHPUCP analysis, which shapes what a resident's DNI will show and therefore how the bathroom rule reads at the door.

Discrimination complaints are heard by INDECOPI, whose consumer-protection chamber dismissed the SmartFit complaint in Resolution 0735-2022; residents have that route but its recent record on restroom complaints is unfavourable.

Since June 2024 official health guidance has dropped pathologising terminology for gender diversity, which affects how trans patients are treated in healthcare settings.

Because sexual orientation and gender identity are not part of the state's crime-registration systems, residents reporting an incident cannot have it registered or prosecuted as a hate crime.

Public venues, businesses and media operating in Huánuco must follow the national signage and content rules, including the ban on inclusive restroom wording and the Article 4 restriction on media and advertising content, with the obscenity minimum raised to four years.

A July 2025 Lima constitutional court struck down an anti-equality decree after an activist legal challenge, giving residents a documented precedent for constitutional litigation against executive measures.
outOfScopeNotes:
Every source in the inventory is national; none contains Huánuco-specific content, so local enforcement patterns, regional government directives and incidents in the department remain unresolved and not sourced.

Whether police, regional health facilities or municipal authorities in Huánuco have issued their own instructions under the April 2025 law is not sourced.

The practical frequency of DNI checks at restroom doors, and any documented challenge to such a check in Huánuco or elsewhere outside the SmartFit case, is unresolved in the inventory.

Departmental breakdowns of the 54 killings and 170 rights-violation cases recorded for 2020 to 2023 are not available in these sources, so the share occurring in Huánuco cannot be stated.

The status of the underlying bills 6506 and 8457 after the February 2025 committee approval, beyond the substance carried by the April 2025 law, is not confirmed here.
